answer:
**QAT lets the model practice under the numerical restrictions it will face later.** During the forward pass, fake quantization rounds and clips values as the deployment quantizer would. The model still keeps trainable high-precision parameters so small updates can accumulate. This differs from training entirely in full precision and quantizing only afterward. [1](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/index.html)

Suppose the quantization step is 0.1. Values 0.21 and 0.24 both round to 0.2. Small changes within that interval do not change the quantized output, so the true derivative of rounding is zero almost everywhere and undefined at transitions. Using that derivative literally would prevent useful gradient learning through the operation.

**The straight-through estimator deliberately uses a surrogate.** It often treats the derivative as one inside the supported range, passing the upstream gradient to the underlying value. Some versions suppress gradients outside clipping limits. This is not the exact derivative of rounding; it is a biased optimization device that allows parameters to adapt to quantization effects.

Check that training simulates deployment's rounding, clipping, scale granularity, and accumulator behavior closely enough. Test the exported low-precision model, not only the fake-quantized training graph. A good training metric can hide differences in the eventual inference kernel. QAT can recover accuracy, but it cannot guarantee arbitrary bit-width reductions without a task-quality cost.

**Technical details and references.**

QAT inserts fake quantization into training: forward rounds/clips values as a target quantizer would, while retaining trainable high-precision parameters. Since the true derivative of rounding is zero almost everywhere, the straight-through estimator substitutes a useful surrogate gradient. [1](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/index.html)

$$\hat x=s\,\operatorname{round}(x/s),\qquad \frac{\partial\hat x}{\partial x}\approx1$$

inside a chosen clipping range, often zero outside. This gradient is biased; it is an optimization heuristic, not the exact derivative. Training can adapt weights and activations to quantization noise. The fake quantizer, scale granularity, rounding, and deployment kernels must match closely. Validate the exported integer/low-precision model, because good fake-quantized training metrics do not guarantee identical deployed behavior.
